questions.prompt: A team is standing up a new workspace that will eventually need Unity Catalog governance (Chapter 4). Which pricing tier must they choose, and why?
options: Premium, because Unity Catalog's role-based access control and audit logging depend on it
Standard, because Unity Catalog is a core feature available at every pricing tier
Trial, because Unity Catalog is only ever enabled during a time-limited evaluation period
Either tier works equally well, since Unity Catalog is configured independently of workspace tier
questions.explain: Standard covers core notebook/cluster/job features with no advanced security controls. Premium adds role-based access control and audit logging — the exact features Unity Catalog depends on — which is why real production workspaces that need governance almost always use Premium, not Standard or the evaluation-only Trial tier.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is true about job clusters, per Lesson 5.
options: A job cluster is created automatically when a scheduled job runs and is terminated immediately afterward
A job cluster costs less per DBU than an all-purpose cluster, since there's no risk of it sitting idle and billing for nothing
Multiple people routinely attach to a job cluster interactively to debug a pipeline together
A job cluster is the right choice for a nightly ETL job that runs the same notebook unattended
A job cluster, once created, stays running indefinitely so the next scheduled run can reuse it
questions.explain: A job cluster is provisioned for exactly one scheduled run and torn down right after, which is why it's priced lower per DBU than an all-purpose cluster and why it's the right fit for an unattended nightly job. Nobody attaches to a job cluster interactively — that's what all-purpose clusters are for — and a job cluster does not persist between runs; each run gets its own fresh cluster.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: no matter which of the four widget types you created, reading its current value back into your code is always done with dbutils.widgets.________("name"), and the result always comes back as a string.
questions.explain: dbutils.widgets.get() reads whatever value currently sits in a widget — text, dropdown, combobox, or multiselect — and always returns it as a string, regardless of the widget's type. dbutils.widgets.text() is the call that creates the widget in the first place, not the one that reads it back.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 8, 10, and 12 to what it actually is.
right: A native, vectorized query engine that accelerates the same PySpark/SQL code, on by default
Workspace-local storage with no Unity Catalog governance attached to it at all
A long-lived credential that authenticates CLI/REST API calls in place of a password
A DBFS path pointing at a real, separate cloud storage container, like an ADLS Gen2 container
questions.explain: DBFS root (dbfs:/FileStore/ and similar) is workspace-local storage with no Unity Catalog governance. A mount is a DBFS path pointing at a real, separate cloud storage container such as ADLS Gen2. A personal access token is the long-lived credential that authenticates CLI/REST API calls instead of a password. Photon is the native, vectorized engine that has accelerated SQL/DataFrame work by default for years.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating and running a scheduled Databricks Job, per Lesson 11, in the correct order.
items: In Jobs & Pipelines, click Create Job
Add a task: pick a notebook and a cluster to run it on, usually a job cluster created fresh for the run
Set a schedule, such as a cron expression or an every-day-at-2-AM picker
Save the job so it runs itself on schedule with nobody present
Check the job's Run history for a Succeeded, Failed, or Running status
questions.explain: Creating a job always starts with Create Job in the Jobs & Pipelines section, then a task is added pointing at a notebook and a cluster (normally a fresh job cluster), then a schedule is set, then the job is saved so it runs unattended. Only after it has actually run does Run history give a real, recorded status to check — not before.

questions.prompt: Notebook A and Notebook B are both attached to the same running cluster. Notebook A runs a cell that creates a DataFrame called trips. What happens when Notebook B then tries to reference trips?
options: It fails — each notebook keeps its own separate variables and temp views, even while sharing the same cluster's compute resources
It succeeds, because any two notebooks attached to the same cluster share one combined in-memory state
It succeeds, but only after Notebook B is manually reattached to the cluster
It fails only because trips was never registered as a temp view with createOrReplaceTempView
questions.explain: Multiple notebooks attached to the same cluster share that cluster's compute resources, but each notebook's session keeps its own isolated variables, DataFrames, and temp views. Notebook A creating trips never makes it visible in Notebook B, regardless of whether it was ever registered as a temp view — shared compute, isolated state.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Databricks Runtime, per Lesson 10.
options: Choosing a Databricks Runtime Version picks the Spark version, OS, and a curated set of libraries and optimizations, not just plain Apache Spark
An LTS version is the right choice for a scheduled production job, since it gets an extended support window
Interactive, exploratory work should always pin to the exact same LTS version a production job uses
Photon is a native, vectorized engine that accelerates the same PySpark/SQL code, and has been on by default for years
Photon requires rewriting existing PySpark code before it can accelerate anything
questions.explain: A Databricks Runtime Version bundles a specific Spark version with the OS and Databricks' own curated libraries and optimizations — it's never just open-source Spark alone. LTS versions get an extended support window, which is why production jobs pin to one; interactive, exploratory work can more safely track the newest version instead. Photon accelerates the exact same PySpark/SQL code unmodified, and has been on by default since 9.1 LTS.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on the compute-creation form, the setting that shuts an idle cluster down after a specified period of inactivity — called out as the single most important real-world cost control on the whole form — is ________ ________.
questions.explain: A running cluster bills by the hour whether or not anyone is using it, so automatic termination — shutting it down after a set period of inactivity — is the single most important cost control on the compute form, and one that's easy to forget when you're focused on getting a notebook working.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what Delta Lake's _delta_log/ folder actually contains and does?
options: It is a sequential, append-only log of numbered JSON commit files, each recording which Parquet files were added or removed — the mechanism behind every ACID guarantee Delta provides
It is a backup copy of every Parquet file in the table, stored in a compressed format for disaster recovery
It is a cache of query results that Spark reuses to speed up repeated reads of the same table
It is a separate relational database that stores the table's rows outside of the Parquet files themselves
It is a lock file that one writer holds exclusively while writing, preventing any other process from reading the table at the same time
It is an index of column statistics only, used exclusively by ZORDER BY to skip files, with no role in writes or concurrency
questions.explain: The _delta_log/ folder is a sequential, append-only sequence of numbered JSON commit files. Each commit records add and remove actions naming exactly which Parquet files are, or are no longer, part of the table's current version. Every guarantee the rest of the chapter covers — atomicity, time travel, safe concurrent MERGE — is reconstructed directly from replaying this log, not from any separate database, cache, or backup.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E sounds plausible because the log IS what enforces Delta's ACID guarantees, but Delta explicitly does not lock the table while writing. Lesson 18's optimistic concurrency model lets writers proceed without waiting for any lock, and only checks for a real conflict against the log at commit time. The log is a record of commits, not a mutex held during a write.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how Delta Lake's ACID guarantees actually work, per Chapter 2.
options: Atomicity means a commit either completes entirely or leaves no trace in the log — never a half-written set of files
Isolation means concurrent writers don't see each other's uncommitted changes
Delta enforces these guarantees by acquiring an exclusive lock on the table for the full duration of every write
Durability relies on the same durability the underlying cloud storage already provides once a commit is written
Consistency means every reader always sees whichever commit is most recent, even one that hasn't finished being written yet
questions.explain: Atomicity, Isolation, and Durability are exactly as Lesson 18 describes them: a commit fully succeeds or leaves no trace, concurrent writers can't see each other's uncommitted work, and once committed, a change is as durable as the cloud storage underneath it. Delta does not lock the table for the duration of a write — it uses optimistic concurrency, letting writers proceed and resolving conflicts only at commit time. Consistency guarantees a valid, complete table state for every reader, which specifically rules out exposing an in-progress, unfinished commit as if it were current.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: by default, Delta Lake's schema enforcement rejects a write whose schema doesn't match the target table — but adding .option("________", "true") to that same write deliberately widens the table's schema to accept a genuinely new column instead of failing.
questions.explain: The mergeSchema write option tells Delta to deliberately widen a table's schema to include a new, additive column rather than rejecting the write as a mismatch. Existing rows get the new column filled with NULL. It still refuses a lossy type change, like a double column suddenly receiving string values — mergeSchema is for growing a schema safely, not for disabling schema enforcement altogether.

questions.prompt: Match each transaction-log or maintenance term to what it actually does.
right: Co-locates rows with similar column values within compacted files, enabling file-level skipping
Marks a file as no longer part of the current version, without necessarily deleting it from disk
A periodic summary Parquet file so a reader doesn't have to replay every commit from the beginning
Marks a Parquet file as now part of the table's current version
questions.explain: An add action marks a Parquet file as part of the table's current version; a remove action marks one as no longer current, without necessarily deleting it from disk right away — exactly what makes time travel possible. A checkpoint is a periodic summary Parquet file so readers don't replay the entire commit history from scratch. ZORDER BY co-locates related rows within already-compacted files so later queries can skip whole files that provably can't match.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order Delta's optimistic concurrency model actually resolves two writers committing at the same time.
items: Writer A and Writer B each read the table at version 5 and begin writing what they each intend to become version 6
Writer A commits first, and its version 6 commit succeeds
Writer B attempts to commit its own version 6 and detects a conflict against the log
Delta checks whether Writer B's change actually conflicts with the change Writer A just committed
If there's no real conflict, Writer B's commit is automatically re-written as version 7; if there is a real conflict, Writer B's write fails with an error to retry
questions.explain: Delta doesn't lock the table to make one writer wait for the other. Both writers proceed optimistically from the same starting version; whichever commits first simply succeeds. The second writer's attempt is then checked against the log for a genuine conflict — if the underlying changes don't actually overlap, its commit is transparently renumbered to the next version; only a real conflict causes a failure that the application is expected to retry.

questions.code:
# Existing Delta table columns: VendorID (string), fare_amount (double)

new_data = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("2", 14.5, "extra_value")],
    ["VendorID", "fare_amount", "unexpected_column"],
)

new_data.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/data/nyc_taxi/delta/trips")
questions.prompt: This write runs against the existing Delta table with no extra write options set. What actually happens, and why?
options: The write fails with an AnalysisException, because unexpected_column isn't part of the table's schema and schema enforcement rejects the mismatch by default
The write succeeds, silently dropping unexpected_column, because Delta ignores any incoming column it doesn't already recognize
The write succeeds, and unexpected_column is automatically added to the table's schema with every existing row's value set to NULL
The write fails, but only because 14.5 can't be stored in a column typed as double
questions.explain: By default, Delta rejects a write whose schema doesn't match the target table's schema, raising an AnalysisException that names the exact mismatch — here, an extra column the table doesn't have. Delta doesn't silently drop unrecognized columns or quietly widen the schema on its own; that widening only happens when mergeSchema is explicitly set, or through an explicit ALTER TABLE.

questions.prompt: A table's VACUUM retention window is left at its default. A write from 10 days ago was later overwritten, and VACUUM has run at least once since then. What happens now when someone runs spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", <that old version>).load(path)?
options: The read fails or returns incomplete results, because VACUUM has already permanently deleted the unreferenced files that version depended on, since they were older than the 7-day retention window
The read succeeds normally, because VACUUM never deletes a file as long as some version number still refers to it, regardless of age
The read succeeds, because time travel reconstructs old data purely from the _delta_log/ JSON files and never actually needs the original Parquet files
The read fails with a schema mismatch error, because VACUUM changes the table's schema as a side effect of deleting old files
questions.explain: VACUUM permanently deletes files no longer referenced by the current version once they're older than the retention window — 7 days by default. A file from 10 days ago that an old version depends on is squarely past that window, so VACUUM can remove it for good. Once that happens, the version that relied on it genuinely becomes unqueryable, which is exactly why time travel is a safety net for recent history, not a permanent backup.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about OPTIMIZE and ZORDER BY, per Lesson 23.
options: OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer, larger ones without changing the table's underlying data or schema
OPTIMIZE itself generates a new entry in the transaction log, with add actions for the compacted files and remove actions for the old small ones
ZORDER BY sorts the table's rows into one single global sort order across every column it names
Running OPTIMIZE after every single write is standard practice for every Delta table, regardless of how often it's updated
ZORDER BY lets a later query filtering on the named column skip whole files that provably contain no matching values
questions.explain: OPTIMIZE rewrites a table's small files into fewer, larger ones with the same data and schema, and it does this as just another Delta commit — add actions for the new compacted files, remove actions for the old small ones. ZORDER BY doesn't produce one literal global sort order; it co-locates rows sharing similar values for the named column(s) within those compacted files, which is what lets a later filter skip whole files that can't match. OPTIMIZE is periodic maintenance scheduled to match a table's update frequency, not something run after every single write.

questions.code:
MERGE INTO trips AS target
USING new_trips AS source
ON target.trip_id = source.trip_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
questions.prompt: A colleague suggests replacing this single MERGE statement with a separate UPDATE for matching rows followed by a separate INSERT for new rows, to make the logic easier to read. What's the real downside of making that change?
options: The two separate statements aren't atomic together — a failure between them can leave the table half-updated, and the matching rows have to be identified manually first instead of inside one statement
There's no real downside — UPDATE and INSERT are simply more efficient individually, since MERGE always scans the entire table twice as a side effect of combining both operations
Separate UPDATE and INSERT statements aren't valid against a Delta table at all, so the replacement wouldn't run
MERGE is only syntactic sugar — Delta runs the exact same two commits internally either way, so there is genuinely no difference in safety
questions.explain: MERGE handles the update-matched / insert-new upsert pattern atomically in one statement. Splitting it into separate UPDATE and INSERT statements means a failure between the two can leave the table in a half-updated state, and it loses MERGE's single ON-based matching — a developer would have to separately figure out which incoming rows are new versus already present before writing the INSERT at all.

questions.prompt: A pipeline writes bronze.trips, then silver.trips from bronze, then gold.daily_revenue from silver. An analyst finds a bug in the gold aggregation logic itself — bronze and silver are both fine. Given medallion architecture's one-directional data flow, what is the correct way to fix the published gold numbers?
options: Rebuild gold.daily_revenue directly from silver.trips using corrected aggregation logic — the normal way gold is produced to begin with
Edit the gold table's rows by hand so the totals match what they should have been
Rebuild silver.trips from the current (wrong) gold.daily_revenue numbers, then regenerate gold from that
Re-ingest bronze.trips from the original source files first, even though the bug is only in the gold aggregation step
questions.explain: Each layer is built FROM the layer before it, one direction, every time — a gold table is never the source for silver, and silver is never rebuilt from gold. Since the bug is only in the aggregation logic, the fix is simply to recompute gold from silver's already-clean data, exactly how gold is normally produced; bronze and silver don't need to be touched at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the silver layer, per this chapter's coverage of casting, deduplication, and conforming.
options: Casting a column's type should happen before deduplicating on it, since dropDuplicates on a string value and a double of the same value would treat them as different, unmatched values
"Conforming" means reconciling naming, units, or categorical values across multiple source systems so that gold never has to know more than one source was ever involved
Silver's job is business-level aggregation with groupBy()/.agg(), shaped for a specific dashboard question
Silver reads directly from the original source files, bypassing bronze entirely
Null-handling in silver typically happens after casting, not before, following the same cast-then-dedupe-then-null-handle order
questions.explain: Casting first ensures later steps compare real typed values rather than strings, which is why cast comes before dedupe and null-handling. Conforming is exactly reconciling multiple sources into one consistent shape. Aggregation with groupBy/.agg() is gold's job, not silver's, and silver reads from bronze (spark.table("bronze.trips")), never straight from the original source files.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a stored value — such as the latest _ingested_at timestamp already processed — used to filter bronze for only rows that arrived since last time, is called a ________.
questions.explain: A watermark is a stored marker of what's already been processed, used to filter a source for only what's newer. Lesson 26's _ingested_at metadata column exists specifically to make this pattern possible — without it, there'd be no reliable way to tell old bronze rows from new ones.

questions.prompt: Match each incremental/streaming term to what it actually does in the medallion pipeline.
right: Bridges a streaming write back to ordinary batch operations, like MERGE, per micro-batch
Holds rows that failed a quality check, kept somewhere inspectable rather than dropped or passed through
Autoloader's streaming source format that tracks which files it has already processed
Where a stream records its processing progress, guaranteeing a file or micro-batch is never processed twice
questions.explain: cloudFiles is Autoloader's self-tracking source format. checkpointLocation is where processing progress is recorded so reruns only pick up genuinely new data. foreachBatch bridges a streaming write back to batch operations like MERGE, which has no native streaming sink. A quarantine table keeps bad rows inspectable instead of silently dropping or blindly keeping them.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of tracing one NYC Taxi trip record through the full medallion pipeline, per the chapter's end-to-end trace, in the correct order.
items: The trip record arrives as one row in a CSV file in the landing folder
Autoloader's cloudFiles source picks up the new file within minutes
The row lands in bronze.trips untouched, with _ingested_at recorded
foreachBatch casts fare_amount to double, checks for duplicates, and applies the quality check
The cleaned row is merged into silver.trips
The gold task aggregates the row into that day's total in gold.daily_revenue
A dashboard queries gold.daily_revenue and shows a number that includes this trip
questions.explain: This is the chapter's own full trace: a file lands, Autoloader ingests it into bronze untouched, foreachBatch cleans and quality-checks it before merging into silver, the gold task aggregates silver into the daily total, and only then does a dashboard query see the trip reflected in a number.

questions.prompt: This bronze-to-silver job is accidentally run a second time for the same process_date after a transient failure triggered a retry. What actually happens, and why?
options: silver.trips ends up with duplicate rows for that date, because mode("append") always adds the written rows rather than checking whether equivalent rows already exist in the target
Nothing changes on the second run, because append automatically skips rows that already exist in the target table
The second run raises an error, because Delta tables refuse to append the same process_date's rows twice
silver.trips is automatically deduplicated whenever it's queried, so the duplicate rows never actually show up in results
questions.explain: append is not idempotent: it has no concept of 'these rows are already there,' so running the exact same batch twice writes the exact same cleaned rows twice, doubling totals downstream. MERGE, matching on the same key used for deduplication, is what makes a rerun safe — it's exactly why the chapter recommends MERGE over append for silver.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about handling late-arriving data in a medallion pipeline, per this chapter.
options: A trip's real-world timestamp (tpep_pickup_datetime) and its bronze arrival timestamp (_ingested_at) can legitimately differ when the source system is delayed
A gold table that only ever processes 'today's new rows' will automatically pick up and correct late data for past dates on its own
Reprocessing a lookback window of recent dates and merging the corrected rows back into gold is a practical way to catch late corrections
Late data can only be handled correctly if bronze filters out malformed or late-looking rows before they're allowed to arrive
Bronze's append-only, keep-everything design is what makes correcting for late data possible at all
questions.explain: Late data is defined by exactly that gap between real-world timestamp and ingestion timestamp. A pipeline that only revisits 'today' never notices a correction for a past date — that's the whole problem a lookback window with MERGE solves. And nothing about bronze's design needs to change for late data, precisely because bronze never filters anything out in the first place; that permanence is what makes reprocessing possible.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: writeStream has no built-in sink that can call MERGE directly, since MERGE is a table-level operation, not a streaming sink. The ________ method bridges this gap by handing each arriving micro-batch to an ordinary Python function as a regular, static DataFrame, where MERGE works exactly as it always has.
questions.explain: foreachBatch is the bridge between streaming writes and ordinary batch operations. Because writeStream has no .mergeStream() method, foreachBatch hands each micro-batch to a normal Python function where a plain DeltaTable MERGE call runs on it like any static DataFrame.

questions.prompt: A silver table has billions of rows, and its corresponding gold aggregate now takes hours to fully recompute on every run with mode("overwrite"). Which approach does this chapter recommend instead, for a gold table at this scale?
options: Switch gold to a MERGE-based pattern that updates only the aggregate rows that could have actually changed, rather than rebuilding the entire table every run
Keep using overwrite exactly as-is, just schedule it to run less often so the cost matters less
Switch gold.daily_revenue to mode("append") so each run only adds today's new totals on top of the existing rows
Skip building a gold table entirely and have the dashboard query silver.trips directly on every page load
questions.explain: overwrite is the simpler default for most gold tables because they're small enough to fully recompute cheaply, but for a genuinely large aggregate built from billions of silver rows, recomputing everything every run gets expensive. The chapter's recommended fix is the same MERGE-based pattern used for silver, updating only the rows that could have actually changed instead of the whole table's history.

questions.prompt: A team runs DROP TABLE on nyc_taxi.bronze.trips (a managed table) and separately on nyc_taxi.bronze.trips_external (an external table pointing at its own Delta files). Which statement correctly describes what happens to the underlying data files in each case?
options: Dropping the managed table deletes its underlying data files along with the catalog registration; dropping the external table only removes the registration, leaving its files on disk untouched
Dropping either table only removes the catalog registration — the underlying data files are never touched in either case
Dropping either table deletes the underlying data files, since DROP TABLE always cleans up storage regardless of table type
Dropping the external table deletes its files along with the registration; dropping the managed table only removes the registration, leaving its files untouched
Both DROP TABLE statements fail with an error, because Unity Catalog requires VACUUM to run on a table before it can be dropped
Whether the underlying files get deleted depends on whether the table format is Delta or Parquet, not on whether the table is managed or external
questions.explain: A managed table's storage location is fully owned by Unity Catalog, so dropping it deletes both the metadata registration and the actual data files. An external table's location is owned by whoever specified it, so Unity Catalog only removes the registration — the files at that LOCATION are completely untouched, since Unity Catalog never claimed their lifecycle.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D states the exact reverse of the real behavior — it swaps which table type actually loses its files. It's the managed table whose files get deleted on DROP TABLE, precisely because Unity Catalog owns its storage location; the external table's files survive because Unity Catalog only ever managed its metadata, never its underlying storage.

questions.code:
CREATE TABLE dev.bronze.trips (VendorID STRING, fare_amount DOUBLE) USING DELTA;
CREATE TABLE prod.bronze.trips (VendorID STRING, fare_amount DOUBLE) USING DELTA;
questions.prompt: dev.bronze.trips and prod.bronze.trips are created with identical schemas. Why can these two tables safely coexist without any naming conflict?
options: They're genuinely separate tables, because the catalog is part of a table's full three-part identity — the same schema.table name in two different catalogs names two different tables
They aren't actually separate tables — Unity Catalog silently merges any writes made under either name into one shared underlying table
They can't actually coexist — creating prod.bronze.trips after dev.bronze.trips already exists raises a naming conflict error
They only avoid conflict because one of the two must be declared as an external table
questions.explain: Under Unity Catalog, a table's real, full name is catalog.schema.table. Because the catalog is part of that identity, dev.bronze.trips and prod.bronze.trips are two completely separate tables that merely happen to share the same schema.table portion of their name — exactly the dev/prod promotion pattern Lesson 39 describes.

questions.prompt: An admin runs only `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE nyc_taxi.gold.daily_revenue TO \`analytics-team\`;` and grants nothing else. Select every true statement about whether analytics-team can now actually query that table.
options: This single GRANT is not enough on its own — analytics-team also needs USE CATALOG on nyc_taxi and USE SCHEMA on gold before the SELECT grant has any effect
If analytics-team is missing USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA, a SELECT query against nyc_taxi.gold.daily_revenue from that group will still fail
Granting SELECT at the table level, the way this GRANT does, is more precise than granting SELECT at the schema level, which would also apply to every future table added to gold
USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are purely a session convenience under access control and have no bearing on whether a GRANT actually works
This single GRANT is sufficient on its own, since SELECT on a specific table is independent of whatever catalog or schema it happens to live in
questions.explain: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are required privileges under access control, not just session shorthand — a user needs both, in addition to SELECT on the specific table, before that SELECT grant does anything at all. Granting at the table level, one table at a time, is more precise than granting at the schema level, which automatically reaches every current and future table in that schema.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is the top-level Unity Catalog container, scoped to a single cloud region, and is typically shared across every workspace attached to that region.
questions.explain: The metastore is the top-level container in Unity Catalog's object hierarchy, scoped to one cloud region. An organization typically has one metastore per region, attached to multiple workspaces, which is exactly why a permission granted once applies everywhere that metastore is attached.

questions.prompt: Match each Unity Catalog governance mechanism from Lessons 43-45 to what it actually does.
right: An automatically-tracked graph of which tables and columns feed which others, built from observing real Spark queries
A function that hides entire rows from a query's result based on who's asking, with no separate copy of the table ever created
Governed, addressable file storage living inside a schema, with a path shape of /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/file
A function that replaces a specific column's returned value per-query, based on the querying user's group membership
questions.explain: A column mask is a function substituting a column's value per-query based on who's asking. A row filter is a function that drops entire rows from the result for some users, same mechanism, different granularity. Lineage is an automatically-built graph of upstream/downstream tables and columns, with zero manual maintenance. A volume is governed file storage inside a schema, addressed as /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/file — DBFS root's real, governed replacement.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from Lesson 40 in the correct order for setting up a brand-new catalog and its bronze/silver/gold schemas from scratch.
items: Run CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS nyc_taxi, optionally with a MANAGED LOCATION
Run USE CATALOG nyc_taxi to set it as the session's current catalog
Run CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS for bronze, silver, and gold inside that catalog
Run SHOW SCHEMAS IN nyc_taxi to confirm all three schemas now actually exist
questions.explain: The catalog has to exist before anything can be created inside it, so CREATE CATALOG runs first. USE CATALOG then sets the session's default so the following CREATE SCHEMA statements don't need the catalog name repeated. Only after bronze, silver, and gold are created does SHOW SCHEMAS make sense, as a confirmation step rather than a setup step.

questions.prompt: A partner company with no Databricks account of its own needs read access to nyc_taxi.gold.daily_revenue. Why is Delta Sharing the right mechanism here instead of an ordinary GRANT?
options: GRANT assumes the recipient is a known principal inside your own metastore; Delta Sharing is built for recipients outside it, readable through the open Delta Sharing protocol with no Databricks account required on their end
GRANT only works for tables inside a medallion architecture, while Delta Sharing is required for any gold-layer table specifically
Delta Sharing replaces GRANT entirely — once a table is added to a share, GRANT/REVOKE privileges on it stop applying altogether
GRANT and Delta Sharing are the same mechanism under two different names; CREATE SHARE is just newer syntax for an ordinary GRANT
questions.explain: GRANT's whole model assumes the recipient is a known user, group, or service principal already inside your metastore. Delta Sharing solves the opposite problem — an external organization with no account in your metastore, possibly no Databricks account at all — by sharing through the open Delta Sharing protocol. Governance from Lessons 42-43 still applies on a shared table; sharing never bypasses it.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly identifies what "Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines" refers to?
options: A brand-new feature with no earlier name, introduced alongside Lakeflow Connect
The current name for what was previously called Delta Live Tables (DLT); @dlt.table is still the actual decorator used in code
A visual, activity-based orchestration tool that replaces Lakeflow Jobs entirely
Databricks' name for Autoloader's file-ingestion mechanism specifically
A renamed version of Unity Catalog's lineage graph feature
The managed connector layer for SaaS applications and database change streams
questions.distractorExplain: Option F describes Lakeflow Connect, not Declarative Pipelines — Connect is the managed-ingestion layer covering databases, SaaS apps, and streaming systems, a separate one of Lakeflow's three unified pieces. Declarative Pipelines is specifically the transformation layer built on the @dlt.table decorator, previously known as Delta Live Tables (DLT).
questions.explain: Lesson 48 states directly that Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines was previously called Delta Live Tables (DLT), and that real current Databricks documentation, job listings, and production code still reference DLT by that older name. @dlt.table (Lesson 51) is the actual decorator you write in code — recognizing DLT and Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines as the same underlying feature matters for reading anything written before the rename.

questions.prompt: Match each piece this course already built in Chapters 1-4 to the Lakeflow product name it now carries, per Lesson 48's table.
questions.explain: Lesson 48's table maps each already-built piece to its Lakeflow name directly: Autoloader becomes Lakeflow Connect (managed ingestion), the foreachBatch/MERGE cleaning logic becomes Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and manually chained jobs/tasks become Lakeflow Jobs (orchestration). Nothing here is new — it's Chapters 1-4 material given a product name and a more declarative expression.

questions.prompt: In this pipeline, how does Lakeflow know that silver_trips must run after bronze_trips, without either dependency being declared in a job's task list?
options: silver_trips() calls dlt.read_stream("bronze_trips"), and that function-to-function reference is itself the entire dependency declaration Lakeflow reads to build the graph
Both functions share the same table_properties value, which Lakeflow uses to infer ordering
The function names are in alphabetical order, so Lakeflow runs them in that order
A separate job task list, maintained elsewhere, explicitly states that Task 2 depends on Task 1
questions.explain: Lesson 50 is explicit: silver_trips() calling dlt.read_stream("bronze_trips") is the entire dependency declaration. Lakeflow builds a real directed graph purely from which function reads which other function's output — nobody writes 'Task 2 depends on Task 1' anywhere; the framework infers the whole bronze to silver to gold order automatically by reading the code.

questions.prompt: Select every statement below that correctly describes @dlt.expect_or_drop, based on Lesson 52.
options: A row that violates the expectation is filtered out before reaching that table
It behaves like Lesson 36's manual quarantine logic, but built into the framework
A single violation under this decorator stops the entire pipeline run
Violations are only logged; the row is kept in the table regardless
It replaces the need to write a separate .filter() call for valid rows by hand
questions.explain: Lesson 52 describes expect_or_drop as DROP enforcement: violating rows are filtered out, directly matching Lesson 36's manual quarantine behavior, now handled by the framework instead of a hand-written .filter() call. Stopping the entire run on a single violation is expect_or_fail's behavior, not expect_or_drop's, and keeping all rows while only logging counts describes plain @dlt.expect (the warn level).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 53 says NYC Taxi data, as this course has used it, arrives in ________ files, which is why triggered mode — not continuous mode — is clearly the right choice for this course's own pipeline.
questions.explain: Lesson 53 states that NYC Taxi trip data arrives in monthly files — genuinely infrequent, bursty ingestion — and that triggered mode, run on a schedule matching that cadence, is clearly correct, since paying for continuously-running compute between monthly files would be pure waste. Continuous mode earns its cost only for sources generating events by the second, like live sensor or transaction streams.

questions.prompt: Lesson 55 lays out an ordered approach for figuring out what broke in a pipeline run. Arrange these three steps in the order Lesson 55 recommends checking them.
items: Graph view — see which table's node shows a failure first in the dependency chain
Per-table metrics — check whether expectations caught it, or the table failed to update at all
Event log — query the actual error message for the specific failing run
questions.explain: Lesson 55 gives this exact order: first the graph view, to see which table's node failed first in the dependency chain; then per-table metrics, to see whether an expectation caught the problem or the table simply failed to update; and only then the event log, queried directly for the actual error message of the specific failing run. This moves from visual overview to metrics to the real error detail.

questions.prompt: A real organization already uses both Azure Data Factory and Lakeflow. Per Lesson 56, which pattern below correctly describes how the two would typically be combined for a nightly load from an on-prem SQL Server?
options: ADF copies data from the on-prem SQL Server into an ADLS Gen2 landing zone, then triggers a Lakeflow Pipeline task to run the bronze-to-silver-to-gold transformation
Lakeflow connects directly to the on-prem SQL Server using a Copy Activity, then hands off to ADF for bronze-to-silver-to-gold transformation
ADF and Lakeflow cannot be used together in the same organization, so one must fully replace the other
ADF performs the row-level casting and deduplication internally, while Lakeflow is used only to schedule the ADF pipeline
questions.explain: Lesson 56's combined pattern is exactly this: an ADF pipeline's Copy Activity moves data from a system Databricks can't reach directly (on-prem SQL Server) into an ADLS Gen2 landing zone, then an activity triggers a Lakeflow Pipeline task for the actual transformation work. ADF's center of gravity is movement between systems; Lakeflow's is transformation within Databricks — 'Copy Activity' is ADF's construct, not Lakeflow's, and transformation logic lives in @dlt.table functions, not inside ADF.
